shouldFix.appliesTo: PTCB-V32-B1 — answered in part by the new fromBootLockdown; the condition it adds is absent from every scope and refusal enumeration
shouldFix.title: fromBootLockdown is a new mandatory fail-closed requirement whose absence refuses a machine, yet inScopeBootConfigs, refusesBootConfigs and unavailableRefuses all omit it, leaving both the refusal standing and the scope narrowing unstated
shouldFix.theRequirement: fromBootLockdown states refusal three times: optionalDataToken says the authenticated Boot#### VariableData 'MUST contain the 8-bit token lockdown=integrity. Missing token refuses'; lockdownNow says the selected token in /sys/kernel/security/lockdown 'MUST be integrity ... Absent file or any other selected token refuses'; and enforcedBootPolicy.fromBootLockdown says 'Absence refuses.' So a machine lacking the token, or whose present kernel does not select integrity, fails qualification.
shouldFix.theOmission: I searched all three scope clauses for the strings lockdown, OptionalData and fromBootLockdown, and all three return zero. inScopeBootConfigs enumerates the in-scope configuration — UEFI firmware, TPM 2.0, TCG2 log, Secure Boot enabled, measured FilePathList, signed transcript matching through each PCR separator, PCR-4 adjacency — and does not mention the lockdown token. refusesBootConfigs enumerates thirteen refusal conditions ending 'Those machines fail qualification', and omits it. unavailableRefuses enumerates fourteen and omits it. All three were rewritten this generation, since the diff touches pathlessCeremony, so the omission is not an untouched remnant.
shouldFix.whyThisMatters: This contract has twice been found to leave a field's standing unreconciled between its own clause and the aggregate refusal lists, at CLAUDE-V30-S1 and again at PTCB-V32-S1, and on both occasions the accepted fix was to make the lists agree. The v30 demotion of runtimeContinuity was signalled in part by removing it from these very lists, which establishes that presence or absence there carries meaning about refusal standing. Under that reading a machine without the token refuses by fromBootLockdown and qualifies by the enumerations, with no precedence sentence reaching the conflict — although this contract now uses precedence sentences in three other places (roleGoverns, specificationGoverns, recomputeDigest.rule GOVERNING, and the transcript matcher's remnant clause).
shouldFix.theUndisclosedNarrowing: The practical effect is larger than a drafting mismatch. Requiring the literal token lockdown=integrity inside the authenticated Boot#### OptionalData excludes any otherwise-conforming machine whose boot option does not carry that token on its command line — including installations that reach integrity lockdown through the Secure Boot state rather than through an explicit parameter. inScopeBootConfigs is the clause that tells a reader which machines this profile expects to qualify, and it does not mention the new requirement, so the narrowing is invisible at the place designed to disclose it. That is the same class of omission I filed at v25 as CLAUDE-V25-S2, where a change to what could qualify was recorded at the mechanism and not at the scope clauses.
shouldFix.whyNotABlocker: Neither reading falsifies an attestation. Under the strict reading the profile over-refuses; under the loose reading it skips a hardening conjunct whose absence does not affect the correctness of the narrowed, disclosed firmware-launched-kernel-package claim, because the authenticity chain does not depend on it. This is a determinacy and disclosure defect of the same family as CLAUDE-V30-S1 and CLAUDE-V32-S1.
shouldFix.requiredRepair: Add the condition to the three enumerations, in the wording they already use: name the missing or non-integrity lockdown token among refusesBootConfigs' and unavailableRefuses' refusal conditions, and state in inScopeBootConfigs that an in-scope boot option carries lockdown=integrity in its authenticated OptionalData and that the present kernel selects integrity. Optionally mark fromBootLockdown with the governing form already used elsewhere. Nothing in the mechanism itself needs to change.

repairsVerified.finding: PTCB-V32-B1 — disclosure does not close the mandatory Linux OS-ABI member
repairsVerified.result: PARTIALLY ADDRESSED, AND HONESTLY SCOPED. I record what the new mechanism does achieve, because it is real. fromBootLockdown places the lockdown=integrity token inside the authenticated Boot#### UEFI_VARIABLE_DATA, which the signed transcript already covers as an EV_EFI_VARIABLE_BOOT row, so the requirement rests on authenticated boot evidence rather than on a present-state read. Since kernel lockdown cannot be lowered once set, that authenticated conjunct establishes for the whole boot that the unsigned kernel-replacement path was denied — which is a genuine monotonic from-launch property of the kind Codex's second option asked for, and a real improvement on the v29 indicators I rejected. It does not extend to a signature-verified replacement, and the contract says so rather than implying otherwise: fromBootLockdown.role states 'It does not authenticate a signed kexec of a different kernel. NT-TCB-DISCLOSE-KEXEC records that residual', g22 repeats that fromBootLockdown 'addresses unsigned kexec only', inScopeBootConfigs still says the profile 'does not authenticate a later kexec or other post-boot kernel replacement', unavailableRefuses still says 'This refusal set does not claim to detect post-boot kexec', and NT-TCB-DISCLOSE-KEXEC is retained unchanged as a non-closing disclosure. Whether a narrowed-and-disclosed residual discharges the mandatory cell is the question Codex and I have answered differently since v30; on the honesty axis I have applied in my own findings, this generation does not overclaim, so I file no blocker against it. My finding above is about where the new requirement is recorded, not about what it proves.

summary: REJECT at 0 blockers and 1 SHOULD-FIX. Custody is clean: subject unmoved at 84c01d00... and 0444 at both ends, HEAD steady, 47/47 chain pins reproduce, both frozen v32 verdicts reproduce with no replacement, 21 changed paths with zero off-roster, reviewGuidance a pure append, Linux still in D-002 slice 1, and all 30 D-096 mentions are refusals once the thirtieth is read in context. My own SHOULD-FIX is repaired with the exact replacement sentence I proposed. Codex's signedEntry finding is closed in full — appearance in preKernelReferences with a four-field join is mandatory for every non-kernel codeBearing row across the five-PCR interval including rows after kernelEvent, the waiver is confined to preimage reconstruction, and those entries must be DIGEST-BOUND against the measured code digest rather than a package archive digest — and the g22 status-token advisory is closed. The new fromBootLockdown deserves credit on its own terms: by placing lockdown=integrity inside the authenticated Boot#### OptionalData that the signed transcript already covers, and relying on lockdown being unable to be lowered once set, it establishes from authenticated boot evidence that the unsigned replacement path was denied for the whole boot. That is a genuine monotonic from-launch property rather than the present-state indicators I rejected at v29, and the contract does not overclaim it: five clauses confine it to unsigned kexec and route the signed residual to NT-TCB-DISCLOSE-KEXEC, which is retained as explicitly non-closing. Whether that narrowed residual discharges the mandatory cell is the standing difference between the two reviewers and I do not adjudicate it here. What I do file is narrower and independent of that dispute. fromBootLockdown refuses a machine three times over — missing token refuses, absent or non-integrity lockdown selection refuses, absence refuses — and yet inScopeBootConfigs, refusesBootConfigs and unavailableRefuses all return zero occurrences of lockdown, OptionalData and fromBootLockdown, though all three were rewritten this generation and each enumerates every other condition. So a machine lacking the token refuses under the mechanism and qualifies under the enumerations, with no precedence sentence reaching the conflict, and the resulting narrowing of which machines can qualify is invisible at the clause designed to disclose scope. Adding the condition to those three lists closes it; nothing in the mechanism needs to change.
